Orozco JM.lab_name: Sabatini Laboratory, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Orozco JM.role: Researcher trained in David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute and MIT who showed that mTORC1 senses glucose through the glycolysis metabolite DHAP
Orozco JM.sub: Harvard/MIT MD-PhD Program; PhD student in the Sabatini laboratory, Whitehead Institute and MIT Department of Biology (papers 2014–2021; at the time of the studies) · undergraduate research in Erin Cram's lab, Northeastern University
story: Jose Orozco is a co-author of four Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute that mapped how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, learns what nutrients a cell has. Sestrin proteins bind the GATOR2 complex to dampen amino acid signalling (CHA2014). A complex named KICSTOR holds the GATOR1 brake at the lysosome so that nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017). A protein named SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a molecule made from the amino acid methionine (GU2017), which links mTORC1 to diet in a way that may matter for why methionine restriction affects aging. And genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that the kinases AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial problems to mTORC1 (CON2021). These are laboratory studies, mostly in cultured cells.

Orozco's own first-author paper, in Nature Metabolism in 2020, answered a question the field had left open: how mTORC1 knows that glucose is present, separately from the energy sensor AMPK. Working in human cells engineered to lack AMPK, the team traced the signal to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a molecule made partway through glycolysis. DHAP is also a starting material for making fats, a process that mTORC1 controls, which gives a reason for the cell to watch it.

Orozco came to the work through the Harvard/MIT MD-PhD Program, which trains doctors who also do research. After two years at Harvard Medical School, Orozco started a PhD as an MIT Biology graduate student in Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute. Before medical school, Orozco studied at Northeastern University and did research there in Erin Cram's lab on the roundworm C. elegans. In a Whitehead Institute podcast recorded during the fifth year of the PhD, Orozco described the DHAP finding and said the plan was to finish the medical degree without further clinical training and to build a research career. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.
Orozco JM.note: Training (Harvard/MIT MD-PhD, Northeastern, Cram lab) confirmed from the Whitehead Institute Biogenesis podcast page; the podcast page uses 'his', the profile text still avoids pronouns. Current position after the PhD still not found.

Jørgensen JO.lab_name: Department of Clinical Medicine (Hormone and Bone Diseases), Aarhus University, and Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (Aarhus, Denmark)
Jørgensen JO.role: Clinical professor of endocrinology at Aarhus University who studies growth hormone, the pituitary and adrenal glands and metabolism in people, and senior author of a trial showing that high-dose resveratrol did not improve metabolism in obese men
Jørgensen JO.sub: Clinical Professor, Department of Clinical Medicine (Hormone and Bone Diseases), Aarhus University · Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital
story: Jens Otto Lunde Jørgensen is the senior author of the Atlas study POU2013, with Morten Møller Poulsen as first author. Resveratrol, a compound from grape skins, had looked promising in rodents, where it seemed to copy some effects of calorie restriction. The Aarhus team tested it properly in people: obese men took a high dose or a placebo for four weeks, and the researchers measured insulin sensitivity, how the body burned fuel, blood pressure and body composition.

None of these changed with resveratrol. The trial was short and small, but it was carefully controlled, and it showed that the rodent results did not carry over to this group of people. A later trial from the same Aarhus groups, with Jørgensen as a co-author, found no benefit of resveratrol in the metabolic syndrome either (2017).

Jørgensen's main research line is growth hormone, the pituitary hormone that drives growth in children and shapes fat, muscle and sugar metabolism in adults. The group studies how the hormone acts in muscle and fat, including in people with acromegaly, the condition caused by too much growth hormone. Recent papers show that excess growth hormone causes reversible scarring (fibrosis) in muscle and fat of patients with acromegaly (2026) and compare methods for measuring body composition in acromegaly (2025). A 2014 study from the resveratrol trial examined growth hormone signalling in muscle and fat of obese people.

Jørgensen is a clinical professor (klinisk lærestolsprofessor) in the Department of Clinical Medicine at Aarhus University, in the unit for hormone and bone diseases. The university profile describes research on hormones and metabolism, especially diseases of the pituitary and adrenal glands, with both clinical studies in patients and laboratory work.
Jørgensen JO.note: Title and ORCID from the Aarhus University staff page (Danish version). CV is linked there but its content was not read, so training is not given.

Tokunaga C.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Tokunaga C.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor, and first author of a 2004 review on how mTOR combines amino acid and energy signals
Tokunaga C.sub: Assistant professor (joshu), Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (KAKEN record 2002–2004), Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: Chiharu Tokunaga is a co-author of the 2002 Cell paper from Kobe University (HARA2002) that, together with a Boston study in the same issue, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The Kobe team showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase and that silencing raptor in worms mimics loss of TOR. Tokunaga is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003), which found that raptor holds these two targets through a short TOS motif and so presents them to the kinase.

In 2004 Tokunaga was first author, with Ken-ichi Yoshino and Kazuyoshi Yonezawa, of a review in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications explaining how mTOR brings together two kinds of information, whether amino acids are available and whether the cell has enough energy. PubMed lists Tokunaga at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University on that review.

Other PubMed records from the same group, from 2000 to 2006, include work on the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work, on a leucine derivative that blocks amino acid signalling to mTOR, on how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway, and on the motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor.

Japan's national research grant database (KAKEN) lists Tokunaga as an assistant professor at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University from 2002 to 2004, with grants on the crosstalk between mTOR, which senses nutrients, and AMPK, which senses the cell's energy level. The record lists no later affiliation, so a current position could not be confirmed.
Tokunaga C.note: KAKEN researcher record 70335462 (Tokunaga Chiharu, Kobe Biosignal Research Center, 2002-2004, keywords mTOR/raptor/TOS motif/AMPK) matches; no later affiliation listed. Not used as lab_url because it is a grant registry, not a profile page.

Burris HA.lab_name: Sarah Cannon Research Institute (Nashville, Tennessee, USA)
Burris HA.role: Medical oncologist who led the Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville as President and Chief Medical Officer, has run hundreds of early-phase cancer drug trials, including the first trial of the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552, and was ASCO President in 2019–2020
Burris HA.sub: President and Chief Medical Officer, Sarah Cannon Research Institute, Nashville (retirement from this role announced for end of 2025, advisory role after) · at Sarah Cannon since 1997 · President, American Society of Clinical Oncology (2019–2020) · earlier Director of Clinical Research, Institute for Drug Development, San Antonio · U.S. Army physician, Brooke Army Medical Center (service ended 1997)
story: Howard Burris is a co-author of two Atlas trial papers about mTOR drugs in cancer. PIC2014 is the final report of BOLERO-2, which added everolimus, a rapamycin-like mTORC1 blocker, to the hormone drug exemestane in women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. The combination kept the cancer in check for longer (7.8 against 3.2 months) but did not significantly lengthen overall survival. SCH2025 was the first trial in patients of RMC-5552, a newer bi-steric drug designed to block mTORC1 fully while sparing mTORC2. In 57 patients with advanced solid tumours, high blood sugar, a typical side effect of older mTOR drugs, was uncommon (4 percent). Without a comparison group, the trial is an early signal, not proof.

Burris joined the Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville in 1997. It became one of the largest centres in the United States for early-phase (phase 1) cancer trials, where new drugs are first given to patients to find a safe dose. PubMed lists him with a Sarah Cannon affiliation on more than 200 trial papers, which shows how many new cancer drugs pass through this kind of centre on the way to approval.

Burris studied at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and at the University of South Alabama College of Medicine. He served as an Army doctor, finishing his service at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio in 1997, and before that directed clinical research at the Institute for Drug Development in San Antonio. At Sarah Cannon he became Chief Medical Officer and Executive Director of the Drug Development Program, and later President and Chief Medical Officer. He was President of the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) for 2019 to 2020. In October 2025 Sarah Cannon announced that he would retire from the President and Chief Medical Officer role at the end of 2025 and stay on as an adviser.

Nomura DK.lab_name: Nomura Lab, Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Nomura DK.role: Chemical biologist and professor at UC Berkeley who uses chemoproteomics to find druggable sites on proteins, including covalent handles that turn ordinary drug molecules into protein degraders
Nomura DK.sub: Professor of Chemical Biology and Molecular Therapeutics, Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, UC Berkeley (assistant professor 2011, associate 2015, professor since 2019) · Director, Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute (since 2017) · Investigator, Innovative Genomics Institute · Postdoc with Benjamin Cravatt, Scripps Research (to 2011) · PhD, UC Berkeley (2008)
story: Daniel Nomura is a co-author of two papers from Roberto Zoncu's lab in this Atlas about cholesterol as a signal for growth. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. SHI2022 found the cholesterol sensor itself, LYCHOS (previously known as GPR155): when cholesterol is high, LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that keeps mTORC1 off, and so lets mTORC1 reach the lysosome. This was shown in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Nomura's own lab works at the border of chemistry and biology. It uses chemoproteomics, methods that use reactive chemical probes and mass spectrometry to map where small molecules can attach to proteins across the whole cell. A 2019 Nature Chemical Biology paper from the lab, with Zoncu lab member Hijai Shin as second author, showed that a compound attaching covalently to the vacuolar H+-ATPase, the proton pump that acidifies lysosomes, switches on autophagy by inhibiting mTORC1. More recently the lab has designed small chemical 'handles' that bind the E3 ligase RNF126 and, when attached to a drug, make the cell destroy the drug's target protein. In 2026 it used an improved handle to degrade BRD4 and the androgen receptor variant AR-V7, which drives drug-resistant prostate cancer.

Nomura studied molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley (BA 2003) and earned a PhD in molecular toxicology there in 2008 with John Casida. Postdoctoral work in chemical biology followed at the Scripps Research Institute with Benjamin Cravatt, who developed many of the chemoproteomic methods the lab now uses. Nomura joined the Berkeley faculty in 2011 and became a full professor in 2019. Today Nomura is Professor of Chemical Biology and Molecular Therapeutics in the Departments of Chemistry and of Molecular and Cell Biology, directs the Novartis-Berkeley Translational Chemical Biology Institute (since 2017) and is an investigator of the Innovative Genomics Institute. Nomura has also co-founded drug discovery companies, including Frontier Medicines.
